name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q01 - Biological role of secondary amino compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following biologically active compounds containing a secondary amino group is clinically used to increase blood pressure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the clinical compound and functional group
According to the NCERT textbook on amines, two biologically active compounds—namely adrenaline and ephedrine—both contain a secondary amino group and are physiological agents used to increase blood pressure.

Step 2: Evaluate the other choices
Novocain is a synthetic amino compound used as an anaesthetic in dentistry, Benadryl is an antihistaminic drug that contains a tertiary amino group, and aniline is a primary aromatic amine used in dye manufacture.

Conclusion:
Ephedrine is the biologically active secondary amine used to elevate blood pressure.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q02 - Clinical dental application of novocain

questiontext.text: Novocain, a synthetic amino compound, is primarily used in medicine as a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the clinical applications described in the textbook
The introduction to amines highlights that Novocain is a synthetic amino derivative widely employed as an anaesthetic in dental procedures.

Step 2: Distinguish from related pharmacological agents
Adrenaline and ephedrine are used to increase blood pressure, Benadryl is an antihistaminic compound, and quaternary ammonium salts are used as surfactants.

Conclusion:
Novocain functions as a local anaesthetic in dentistry.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q03 - Nature of amino group in benadryl

questiontext.text: The antihistaminic drug Benadryl contains which of the following functional groups?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Review the functional groups of drugs cited in the chapter
The NCERT text explicitly specifies that the well-known antihistaminic drug Benadryl contains a tertiary amino group.

Step 2: Contrast with other amino drugs
Adrenaline and ephedrine possess secondary amino groups, whereas quaternary ammonium salts are cationic surfactants.

Conclusion:
Benadryl contains a tertiary amino group.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q04 - Hybridization and geometry of amine nitrogen

questiontext.text: In aliphatic amines, the nitrogen atom is trivalent, carries an unshared electron pair, and exhibits which hybridization and molecular geometry?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine the steric number of nitrogen
In amines, nitrogen forms three covalent \(sp^3\)-bonds (with carbon or hydrogen) and retains one unshared electron pair (lone pair). The steric number is \(3 + 1 = 4\), corresponding to \(sp^3\) hybridization.

Step 2: Deduce the molecular shape
Although the electron pair arrangement is tetrahedral, the molecular geometry (considering only atomic nuclei) is pyramidal due to the presence of the lone pair.

Conclusion:
The nitrogen atom exhibits \(sp^3\) hybridization and the amine molecule has a pyramidal geometry.

answer.text: \(sp^2\) hybridization with a trigonal planar geometry

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q05 - Bond angle deviation in trimethylamine

questiontext.text: In trimethylamine, the \(\mathrm{C-N-C}\) bond angle is \(108^{\circ}\), which is less than the normal tetrahedral angle of \(109.5^{\circ}\). This reduction is primarily caused by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the electronic distribution around nitrogen
In trimethylamine, nitrogen is \(sp^3\) hybridised with three bonding pairs and one unshared electron pair.

Step 2: Apply VSEPR theory
According to VSEPR theory, lone pair-bond pair repulsions are stronger than bond pair-bond pair repulsions. This pushes the three \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bonds closer together, decreasing the \(\mathrm{C-N-C}\) angle from \(109.5^{\circ}\) to \(108^{\circ}\).

Conclusion:
The compression of the bond angle is due to repulsion exerted by the unshared electron pair on the bonding electron pairs.

answer.text: Repulsion between the unshared electron pair and bonding electron pairs
Steric repulsion between bulky methyl groups opening the angle
The presence of \(d\)-orbitals on the nitrogen atom
Resonance delocalization of the lone pair into the methyl groups

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q06 - Distinction between simple and mixed amines

questiontext.text: Which of the following amines is classified as a 'simple' secondary amine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the definition of simple and mixed amines
Amines are classified as 'simple' when all the alkyl or aryl groups attached to the nitrogen atom are identical, and 'mixed' when the attached groups are different.

Step 2: Analyze the given compounds
In diethylamine \((\mathrm{C_2H_5-NH-C_2H_5})\), both alkyl substituents on the secondary nitrogen are ethyl groups, making it a simple secondary amine. In contrast, N-methylethanamine contains a methyl and an ethyl group, making it a mixed amine.

Conclusion:
Diethylamine is a simple amine because both alkyl groups attached to the nitrogen are identical.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q07 - Systematic IUPAC naming of hexamethylenediamine compound

questiontext.text: What is the systematic IUPAC name for hexamethylenediamine, \(\mathrm{H_2N-(CH_2)_6-NH_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the IUPAC nomenclature rule for polyamines
When two or more amino groups are attached to the parent alkane chain, the positions of the carbon atoms bearing the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) groups are specified by locants, the prefix 'di' is attached to amine, and the terminal letter 'e' of the alkane suffix is retained.

Step 2: Apply to hexamethylenediamine
The parent hydrocarbon containing six saturated carbons is hexane. With amino groups at carbons 1 and 6, the name is hexane-1,6-diamine.

Conclusion:
The systematic IUPAC name is hexane-1,6-diamine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q08 - Systematic IUPAC nomenclature of unsaturated allylamine

questiontext.text: What is the IUPAC name of allylamine, having the structure \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_2-NH_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Number the principal chain
The principal functional group is the amine (\(-\mathrm{NH_2}\)), which takes priority for lowest locant over the double bond. Carbon 1 is therefore the carbon bearing the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group: \(\mathrm{CH_2(1)-CH(2)=CH_2(3)}\) is numbered from the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) bearing end.

Step 2: Assign locants to the unsaturation and functional group
The chain contains 3 carbons (prop). The double bond is between C2 and C3 (hence '2-en'), and the amine is at C1. Dropping the terminal 'e' from 'prop-2-ene' gives prop-2-en-1-amine.

Conclusion:
The systematic IUPAC name of allylamine is prop-2-en-1-amine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q09 - IUPAC naming of N N diethylbutan 1 amine

questiontext.text: According to IUPAC rules, what is the systematic name of \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2-N(C_2H_5)_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the longest continuous carbon chain attached to nitrogen
The longest carbon chain attached to the nitrogen atom contains 4 carbons (butan-1-amine).

Step 2: Designate remaining substituents
The two remaining groups attached to nitrogen are ethyl groups. They are designated by the locant 'N', yielding 'N,N-diethyl'.

Step 3: Assemble the complete IUPAC name
Combining the substituents with the parent alkanamine gives N,N-diethylbutan-1-amine.

Conclusion:
The IUPAC name of the compound is N,N-diethylbutan-1-amine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q10 - Total isomeric amines for molecular formula C4H11N

questiontext.text: How many total structural isomeric amines (including primary, secondary, and tertiary) are possible for the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Count primary (1°) amine isomers
For primary amines (\(\mathrm{C_4H_9NH_2}\)), there are 4 butyl group isomers: butan-1-amine, butan-2-amine, 2-methylpropan-1-amine, and 2-methylpropan-2-amine (4 isomers).

Step 2: Count secondary (2°) amine isomers
For secondary amines (\(\mathrm{R-NH-R'}\)), with 4 carbons total: N-methylpropan-1-amine, N-methylpropan-2-amine, and N-ethylethanamine (3 isomers).

Step 3: Count tertiary (3°) amine isomers
For tertiary amines (\(\mathrm{R_3N}\)), the only distribution of 4 carbons is N,N-dimethylethanamine (1 isomer).

Step 4: Calculate total structural isomers
Total structural isomers = \(4 + 3 + 1 = 8\).

Conclusion:
There are exactly 8 isomeric amines corresponding to \(\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q11 - Advantage of Fe and HCl for reduction

questiontext.text: In the industrial reduction of nitro compounds to primary amines, reduction using iron scrap and hydrochloric acid (\(\mathrm{Fe / HCl}\)) is preferred over other metal-acid combinations primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State the governing chemical principle
The NCERT textbook explicitly explains that reduction with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid is preferred because the \(\mathrm{FeCl_2}\) formed during the reduction reaction undergoes hydrolysis to release hydrochloric acid.

Step 2: Evaluate the stoichiometric consequence
Because \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is regenerated *in situ*, only a small amount of hydrochloric acid is needed to initiate the reaction, making it highly economical.

Conclusion:
The process is preferred because \(\mathrm{FeCl_2}\) hydrolyses to release \(\mathrm{HCl}\), necessitating only a small initiating amount of acid.

answer.text: Iron acts as a stronger oxidising agent than tin
The reaction does not release any exothermic heat
\(\mathrm{FeCl_2}\) formed gets hydrolysed to regenerate \(\mathrm{HCl}\), requiring only a catalytic initiation amount of acid
It prevents the formation of any primary amine products

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q12 - Halide reactivity order in ammonolysis

questiontext.text: During the ammonolysis of alkyl halides, what is the correct order of reactivity of different alkyl halides with amines?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Consider the carbon-halogen bond strength
Ammonolysis involves the nucleophilic displacement of a halide ion by cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond. The bond dissociation enthalpy decreases in the order \(\mathrm{C-Cl > C-Br > C-I}\).

Step 2: Relate to leaving group ability
Iodide is the largest and weakest conjugate base, making it the best leaving group. Hence, the rate of nucleophilic substitution is highest for alkyl iodides and lowest for alkyl chlorides.

Conclusion:
The order of reactivity is \(\mathrm{R-I > R-Br > R-Cl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q13 - Conditions to obtain primary amine in ammonolysis

questiontext.text: Ammonolysis of an alkyl halide typically produces a mixture of primary, secondary, and tertiary amines alongside quaternary ammonium salts. To obtain the primary amine as the major product, which reaction condition must be employed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the competitive nucleophilic attack
When ammonia reacts with an alkyl halide, a primary amine is formed. The primary amine is also a nucleophile and can compete with ammonia to react with unreacted alkyl halide to form secondary and tertiary amines.

Step 2: Apply mass action
If a large excess of ammonia is present, the probability of an alkyl halide molecule colliding with and reacting with an ammonia molecule is far greater than colliding with the newly formed primary amine.

Conclusion:
Taking a large excess of ammonia yields primary amine as the major product.

answer.text: Carry out the reaction at very low temperatures below 273 K
Add an equimolar quantity of tertiary amine

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q14 - Ascent of amine series using nitriles

questiontext.text: Which of the following reaction sequences accomplishes the 'ascent of amine series' to convert chloroethane into propan-1-amine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the structural requirement
Chloroethane contains two carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl}\)), whereas propan-1-amine contains three carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)). This represents an ascent of the series (introduction of one extra carbon atom).

Step 2: Trace the nitrile pathway
Nucleophilic displacement of chloride by cyanide using ethanolic \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) forms propanenitrile (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2C\equiv N}\)). Subsequent reduction with \(\mathrm{H_2 / Ni}\) or \(\mathrm{Na(Hg) / C_2H_5OH}\) reduces the nitrile group to a primary amino group (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)).

Conclusion:
Treatment with ethanolic \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) followed by reduction with \(\mathrm{H_2 / Ni}\) synthesizes propan-1-amine from chloroethane.

answer.text: Reaction with ethanolic \(\mathrm{NaCN}\) followed by reduction with \(\mathrm{H_2 / Ni}\)
Reaction with \(\mathrm{KNO_2}\) followed by reduction with \(\mathrm{Fe / HCl}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q15 - Product of ethanamide reduction with LiAlH4

questiontext.text: Reduction of ethanamide with lithium aluminium hydride (\(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\)) followed by aqueous work-up produces:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the reaction of amides with LiAlH4
The reduction of an aliphatic amide \(\mathrm{R-CONH_2}\) with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) followed by hydrolysis reduces the carbonyl group (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)) to a methylene group (\(\mathrm{-CH_2-}\)) without changing the total carbon count.

Step 2: Apply to ethanamide
Ethanamide (\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\)) has two carbons. Its reduction yields \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2NH_2}\) (ethanamine).

Conclusion:
Reduction of ethanamide with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) gives ethanamine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q16 - Inability of Gabriel synthesis to produce aniline

questiontext.text: Aromatic primary amines such as aniline cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the mechanism of Gabriel synthesis
Gabriel synthesis involves the nucleophilic attack of the potassium phthalimide anion on an organic halide via an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) pathway.

Step 2: Evaluate aryl halide reactivity
In aryl halides, the lone pairs on the halogen are conjugated with the benzene ring, imparting partial double-bond character to the carbon-halogen bond. Additionally, steric hindrance and electrostatic repulsion by the aromatic \(\pi\)-cloud prevent nucleophilic substitution by the bulky phthalimide anion.

Conclusion:
Aromatic primary amines cannot be synthesized because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion.

answer.text: Phthalimide cannot form a potassium salt with ethanolic KOH
Aromatic amines are decomposed by alkaline hydrolysis
Potassium phthalimide is insoluble in all organic solvents
Aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the phthalimide anion under normal conditions

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q17 - Carbon count change in Hoffmann bromamide reaction

questiontext.text: In the Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction, the primary amine formed has:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the degradation reaction stoichiometry
The general equation is: \(\mathrm{R-CONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \rightarrow R-NH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O}\).

Step 2: Track the carbonyl carbon
The carbonyl carbon of the amide is eliminated as carbonate (\(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\)), and the \(\mathrm{R}\) group migrates directly to the nitrogen atom.

Conclusion:
The resulting amine contains one carbon atom less than the parent amide.

answer.text: One carbon atom less than the starting amide
One carbon atom more than the starting amide
The same number of carbon atoms as the starting amide
Two carbon atoms less than the starting amide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q18 - Starting amide for propanamine in Hoffmann degradation

questiontext.text: Which carboxylic acid amide must be treated with bromine and aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) in the Hoffmann bromamide reaction to synthesize propan-1-amine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the product and its carbon count
Propan-1-amine contains three carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2}\)).

Step 2: Determine the required precursor
Because Hoffmann bromamide degradation eliminates the carbonyl carbon, the starting amide must contain one more carbon atom than the amine product: \(3 + 1 = 4\) carbon atoms.

Step 3: Identify the four-carbon amide
The four-carbon straight-chain amide is butanamide (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CONH_2}\)).

Conclusion:
Butanamide is the starting amide needed to yield propan-1-amine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q19 - Product of benzamide in Hoffmann degradation

questiontext.text: When benzamide (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\)) is heated with bromine and ethanolic potassium hydroxide, the organic product formed is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the functional groups involved
Benzamide contains a phenyl ring directly attached to a carbonyl amide group: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CONH_2}\).

Step 2: Apply the migration mechanism
In Hoffmann degradation, the aryl group (phenyl) migrates from the carbonyl carbon directly to the nitrogen atom while the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate.

Step 3: Determine the product
The resulting molecule is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2}\), which is aniline (benzenamine).

Conclusion:
Hoffmann degradation of benzamide produces aniline.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q20 - Colour change of arylamines on storage

questiontext.text: Pure aniline and other arylamines are usually colourless liquids or solids, but they frequently turn dark or coloured upon prolonged storage due to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the physical properties of arylamines
The NCERT textbook explicitly notes: 'Aniline and other arylamines are usually colourless but get coloured on storage due to atmospheric oxidation.'

Step 2: Recognize the chemical susceptibility
The high electron density on the benzene ring donated by the amino group makes arylamines particularly susceptible to aerial oxidation into quinonoid and other coloured degradation products.

Conclusion:
The colour change observed upon storage is caused by atmospheric oxidation.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q21 - Solubility comparison between butanol and butanamine

questiontext.text: Considering the Pauling electronegativities of nitrogen (3.0) and oxygen (3.5), butan-1-ol is more soluble in water than butan-1-amine because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Compare electronegativity values
Oxygen has an electronegativity of 3.5, whereas nitrogen has an electronegativity of 3.0. The electronegativity difference \(\Delta \chi\) between oxygen and hydrogen (\(3.5 - 2.1 = 1.4\)) is greater than that between nitrogen and hydrogen (\(3.0 - 2.1 = 0.9\)).

Step 2: Relate bond polarity to hydrogen bonding strength
Because the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond is significantly more polar than the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond, the intermolecular hydrogen bonds formed between the hydroxyl group of butan-1-ol and water are much stronger than those formed by the amino group of butan-1-amine.

Conclusion:
Alcohols are more soluble in water than the corresponding amines because they form stronger hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

answer.text: The \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond is more polar than the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond, enabling alcohols to form stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonds with water
Butan-1-amine has a larger hydrophobic hydrocarbon chain than butan-1-ol
Butan-1-ol forms ionic bonds with water molecules
Nitrogen forms stronger coordinate bonds with water than oxygen

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q22 - Boiling point trend among isomeric butylamines

questiontext.text: For isomeric amines with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}\), what is the correct decreasing order of boiling points?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate hydrogen bonding capability
Primary amines have two hydrogen atoms attached to nitrogen (\(-\mathrm{NH_2}\)), allowing extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Secondary amines have only one hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen (\(>\mathrm{NH}\)), resulting in fewer hydrogen bonds.

Step 2: Evaluate tertiary amines
Tertiary amines have no hydrogen atoms attached to nitrogen (\(>\mathrm{N-}\)), preventing them from forming intermolecular hydrogen bonds with each other.

Step 3: Relate to boiling points
Stronger and more extensive intermolecular association leads to higher boiling points: \(\text{Primary} (350.8\,\mathrm{K}) > \text{Secondary} (329.3\,\mathrm{K}) > \text{Tertiary} (310.5\,\mathrm{K})\).

Conclusion:
The boiling point order of isomeric amines is Primary > Secondary > Tertiary.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q23 - Boiling point comparison of similar molar mass compounds

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly arranges \(n\)-butane (molar mass 58), butan-1-amine (molar mass 73), and butan-1-ol (molar mass 74) in increasing order of their boiling points?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify intermolecular forces in each compound
\(n\)-Butane is non-polar and experiences only weak van der Waals dispersion forces. Butan-1-amine undergoes intermolecular hydrogen bonding via its \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group. Butan-1-ol undergoes stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonding due to its more polar \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group.

Step 2: Compare experimental boiling points
The boiling points are: \(n\)-butane (\(\sim 272.5\,\mathrm{K}\)), butan-1-amine (\(350.8\,\mathrm{K}\)), and butan-1-ol (\(390.3\,\mathrm{K}\)).

Conclusion:
The increasing order of boiling points is \(n\)-butane < butan-1-amine < butan-1-ol.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q24 - Relationship between base strength and pKb

questiontext.text: How is the basic strength of an amine related to its basicity constant \(K_b\) and \(\mathrm{p}K_b\) value?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: State the mathematical definition of pKb
\(\mathrm{p}K_b = -\log_{10} K_b\).

Step 2: Relate equilibrium to basic strength
A stronger base ionizes to a greater extent in water to produce hydroxide ions, giving a higher equilibrium concentration of products and therefore a larger \(K_b\).

Step 3: Evaluate the logarithmic negative scale
Because \(\mathrm{p}K_b\) is the negative logarithm of \(K_b\), a larger \(K_b\) results in a smaller numerical value for \(\mathrm{p}K_b\).

Conclusion:
A stronger base is characterized by a larger \(K_b\) and a smaller \(\mathrm{p}K_b\).

answer.text: A stronger base has a smaller \(K_b\) and a smaller \(\mathrm{p}K_b\)
A stronger base has a larger \(K_b\) and a larger \(\mathrm{p}K_b\)
A stronger base has a smaller \(K_b\) and a larger \(\mathrm{p}K_b\)
A stronger base has a larger \(K_b\) and a smaller \(\mathrm{p}K_b\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q25 - Gas phase basicity order of alkylamines

questiontext.text: In the gaseous phase, where solvent effects are absent, what is the correct decreasing order of basicity of aliphatic amines and ammonia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the governing factor in the gas phase
In the gas phase, there is no solvation of the resulting ammonium cations. The basic strength is determined entirely by the electron-releasing inductive (+I) effect of alkyl groups.

Step 2: Analyze inductive charge stabilization
Each alkyl group pushes electron density toward nitrogen, increasing the availability of the lone pair and dispersing the positive charge in the conjugate acid. Three alkyl groups provide the maximum +I effect, followed by two, then one.

Conclusion:
In the gas phase, basicity follows: tertiary amine > secondary amine > primary amine > ammonia.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Tertiary\ amine > Secondary\ amine > Primary\ amine > NH_3}\)
\(\mathrm{Secondary\ amine > Tertiary\ amine > Primary\ amine > NH_3}\)
\(\mathrm{Primary\ amine > Secondary\ amine > Tertiary\ amine > NH_3}\)
\(\mathrm{NH_3 > Primary\ amine > Secondary\ amine > Tertiary\ amine}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q26 - Aqueous basicity order of ethylamines

questiontext.text: In aqueous solution, the decreasing order of basic strength for ethyl-substituted amines and ammonia is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the competing factors in aqueous medium
In water, basicity is governed by a combined interplay of inductive effect (+I), solvation stabilization of the substituted ammonium cation via hydrogen bonding, and steric hindrance to hydration.

Step 2: Evaluate the balance for ethyl groups
For the larger ethyl group, the inductive effect of the alkyl groups is dominant enough that the tertiary amine is more basic than the primary amine, but steric hindrance restricts solvation of the tertiary cation relative to the secondary cation.

Step 3: State the experimental order
The experimental order in aqueous solution corresponds to secondary (2°) > tertiary (3°) > primary (1°) > ammonia: \((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} > (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} > \mathrm{NH_3}\).

Conclusion:
The correct decreasing order of basicity in aqueous solution is diethylamine > triethylamine > ethylamine > ammonia.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q27 - Aqueous basicity order of methylamines

questiontext.text: In aqueous solution, the decreasing order of basic strength for methyl-substituted amines and ammonia is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the governing principles in aqueous phase
The stability of the conjugate ammonium cation in water depends on both electron release (+I) and solvation energy by hydrogen bonding. Solvation stability follows \(1^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 3^{\circ}\).

Step 2: Evaluate the balance for methyl groups
Because the methyl group is small, solvation stabilization is very effective for the primary cation (\(\mathrm{CH_3NH_3^+}\)). As a result, the primary amine surpasses the tertiary amine (\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N}\)), where solvation is diminished.

Step 3: State the experimental aqueous order
The experimental order is secondary (2°) > primary (1°) > tertiary (3°) > ammonia: \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{NH} > \mathrm{CH_3NH_2} > (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N} > \mathrm{NH_3}\).

Conclusion:
The decreasing order of basic strength is dimethylamine > methylamine > trimethylamine > ammonia.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q28 - Reason for lower basicity of aniline

questiontext.text: The \(\mathrm{p}K_b\) value of aniline is 9.38, whereas that of ammonia is 4.75, showing that aniline is a significantly weaker base. This is primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the resonance structures of aniline
In aniline, the unshared electron pair on the nitrogen atom is in conjugation with the aromatic \(\pi\)-system. Aniline is a resonance hybrid of five contributing structures, with partial double-bond character in the \(\mathrm{C-N}\) bond and negative charge localized at ortho and para positions.

Step 2: Examine the anilinium cation
Protonation gives the anilinium ion (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_3^+}\)), which has no lone pair to delocalize and possesses only two Kekule resonating structures.

Step 3: Compare relative stabilities
Aniline is far more stabilized by resonance than the anilinium ion, creating an unfavorable equilibrium for proton acceptance.

Conclusion:
Aniline is weaker because its unshared electron pair is delocalized over the aromatic ring, reducing its availability for protonation.

answer.text: The anilinium ion possesses five resonating structures whereas aniline has only two
The benzene ring exerts a strong +I inductive effect on the amino group
The lone pair on nitrogen is delocalized over the benzene ring through resonance, making it less available for protonation

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q29 - Substituent effects on aromatic amine basicity

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly arranges aniline, \(p\)-toluidine, and \(p\)-nitroaniline in increasing order of their basic strength?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the substituent effect in p-nitroaniline
The nitro group (\(-\mathrm{NO_2}\)) is strongly electron-withdrawing through both \(-I\) and \(-R\) effects, significantly reducing electron density on the nitrogen atom and destabilizing the conjugate acid. Thus, \(p\)-nitroaniline is the weakest base.

Step 2: Analyze the substituent effect in p-toluidine
The methyl group (\(-\mathrm{CH_3}\)) is electron-releasing through \(+I\) and hyperconjugation, increasing electron density on nitrogen and stabilizing the conjugate cation. Thus, \(p\)-toluidine is more basic than aniline.

Step 3: Combine the trend
The increasing order of basic strength is \(p\)-nitroaniline < aniline < \(p\)-toluidine.

Conclusion:
The correct increasing order is \(p\)-nitroaniline < aniline < \(p\)-toluidine.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q30 - Separation of amines using mineral acids

questiontext.text: Amines react with mineral acids to form substituted ammonium salts. This reaction serves as the basis for separating amines from water-insoluble non-basic organic compounds because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the nature of amine salts
Amines react with mineral acids like \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to form ionic alkylammonium salts (e.g., \(\mathrm{RNH_3^+ Cl^-}\)).

Step 2: Evaluate solubility characteristics
Being ionic salts, they dissolve readily in polar solvents like water but are insoluble in non-polar organic solvents like ether. In contrast, neutral non-basic organic compounds remain in the organic phase.

Step 3: Regeneration of free amine
Treating the aqueous phase containing the ammonium salt with a strong base (such as \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) regenerates the uncharged free amine.

Conclusion:
Separation is achieved because amine salts are water-soluble and ether-insoluble.

answer.text: Amine salts are volatile liquids that boil off below room temperature
Amine salts are ionic and soluble in water, but insoluble in organic solvents such as ether
Non-basic organic compounds dissolve preferentially in dilute aqueous hydrochloric acid
Amine salts spontaneously precipitate as insoluble solids from all aqueous media

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q31 - Role of pyridine in acylation of amines

questiontext.text: The acylation of primary or secondary amines with acetyl chloride is typically carried out in the presence of a base stronger than the amine, such as pyridine. What is the primary role of pyridine in this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze the acylation reaction equation
\(\mathrm{R-NH_2 + CH_3COCl \rightleftharpoons R-NHCOCH_3 + HCl}\).

Step 2: Identify the equilibrium behavior
The reaction produces \(\mathrm{HCl}\), which can protonate unreacted amine into an unreactive ammonium salt and push the equilibrium backwards.

Step 3: Apply Le Chatelier's principle
Pyridine is a base stronger than the amine; it reacts with \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to form pyridinium chloride, effectively removing the acid byproduct and driving the equilibrium toward product formation.

Conclusion:
Pyridine neutralizes \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and shifts the equilibrium forward.

answer.text: It acts as a phase-transfer catalyst to hydrolyse the amide product
It protonates the amine to convert it into a stronger nucleophile
It removes the \(\mathrm{HCl}\) formed during the reaction, thereby shifting the reversible equilibrium to the right
It reduces the acyl chloride directly to an aldehyde

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q32 - Reaction of methanamine with benzoyl chloride

questiontext.text: What is the product of the reaction between methanamine and benzoyl chloride (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the reactants
Methanamine is \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\) and benzoyl chloride is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl}\).

Step 2: Trace the nucleophilic substitution
The amino nitrogen attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to form an amide: \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2 + C_6H_5COCl \rightarrow CH_3NHCOC_6H_5 + HCl}\).

Step 3: Assign the IUPAC name
The acyl parent is benzamide and the substituent on nitrogen is a methyl group, giving N-methylbenzamide.

Conclusion:
The product formed is N-methylbenzamide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q33 - Scope of the carbylamine reaction

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds will give a positive carbylamine test (forming an extremely foul-smelling isocyanide upon heating with chloroform and ethanolic \(\mathrm{KOH}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the requirement for the carbylamine reaction
The carbylamine reaction is specific only to primary amines (both aliphatic and aromatic). Secondary and tertiary amines do not undergo this reaction because they lack two hydrogen atoms on the nitrogen atom.

Step 2: Examine the classes of given compounds
Aniline (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)) is a primary aromatic amine. N-Methylaniline is a secondary amine, N,N-dimethylaniline is a tertiary amine, and diethylamine is a secondary aliphatic amine.

Conclusion:
Only aniline gives a positive carbylamine test.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q34 - Products from primary aliphatic amine and nitrous acid

questiontext.text: When a primary aliphatic amine reacts with nitrous acid (prepared *in situ* from \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\)), which products are quantitatively liberated?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Follow the reaction of primary aliphatic amines with HNO2
Primary aliphatic amines react with nitrous acid to generate alkyldiazonium salts: \(\mathrm{R-NH_2 + HNO_2 \rightarrow [R-N_2^+ Cl^-]}\).

Step 2: Evaluate the stability of alkyldiazonium salts
Alkyldiazonium salts lack resonance stabilization and decompose spontaneously, even at low temperatures, liberating nitrogen gas quantitatively and generating carbocations that react with water to form alcohols.

Step 3: Relate to analytical application
The quantitative evolution of \(\mathrm{N_2}\) gas in this reaction is widely used in the analytical estimation of amino acids and proteins.

Conclusion:
The reaction yields an alcohol and quantitatively liberates nitrogen gas.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q35 - Hinsberg reaction product of primary amine

questiontext.text: When ethanamine reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride (Hinsberg's reagent), N-ethylbenzenesulphonamide is formed. Why does this product dissolve in aqueous potassium hydroxide?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the product structure
The reaction yields N-ethylbenzenesulphonamide: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-SO_2-NH-C_2H_5}\).

Step 2: Examine the hydrogen atom on nitrogen
The nitrogen atom still carries one hydrogen atom. This hydrogen is strongly acidic because the adjacent sulphonyl group (\(-\mathrm{SO_2-}\)) is intensely electron-withdrawing, stabilizing the resulting conjugate anion.

Step 3: Evaluate alkali solubility
Because of this acidic hydrogen, the sulphonamide readily donates a proton to aqueous base (such as \(\mathrm{KOH}\) or \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) to form a soluble potassium or sodium salt.

Conclusion:
The product dissolves in alkali because the hydrogen attached to the sulphonamide nitrogen is strongly acidic.

answer.text: It undergoes complete alkaline hydrolysis to yield benzene and ethylamine
The sulphonamide acts as a strong Lewis base that coordinates with potassium ions
The hydrogen attached to the nitrogen atom is strongly acidic due to the strong electron-withdrawing sulphonyl group
The benzene ring possesses high electron density that interacts with hydroxide ions

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q36 - Behavior of secondary amines with Hinsberg reagent

questiontext.text: In the Hinsberg test for distinguishing amines, a secondary amine reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to yield a sulphonamide that is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the reaction of a secondary amine
A secondary amine (e.g., \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\)) reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to form an N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2-N(C_2H_5)_2}\).

Step 2: Analyze the nitrogen atom of the product
Since all hydrogen atoms originally on nitrogen were substituted, there is no hydrogen atom attached to nitrogen in the resulting sulphonamide.

Step 3: Determine solubility in alkali
Lacking an acidic hydrogen, it cannot form a salt with aqueous alkali and therefore remains insoluble in aqueous base.

Conclusion:
The sulphonamide formed from a secondary amine is insoluble in alkali because it has no hydrogen on nitrogen.

answer.text: Soluble in alkali because it forms an acidic zwitterion
Unreactive because secondary amines do not possess nucleophilic nitrogen
A coloured azo dye that precipitates upon acidification
Insoluble in alkali because it contains no acidic hydrogen atom on nitrogen

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q37 - Product of aniline reaction with bromine water

questiontext.text: When aniline is treated with bromine water at room temperature, which precipitate is rapidly formed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate the activating power of the amino group
The amino group (\(-\mathrm{NH_2}\)) is an exceptionally powerful activating and ortho/para-directing group due to strong resonance donation of the nitrogen unshared electron pair into the aromatic ring.

Step 2: Analyze reaction conditions
In aqueous medium, aniline reacts vigorously with bromine water without requiring any Lewis acid catalyst, undergoing rapid bromination at all activated positions (both ortho positions and the para position).

Step 3: State the product
The reaction quantitatively produces a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

Conclusion:
Aniline reacts with bromine water to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q38 - Control of aniline ring reactivity by acetylation

questiontext.text: To prepare 4-bromoaniline as the major product from aniline, the activating effect of the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is controlled by acetylating aniline with acetic anhydride before bromination. Why does acetylation reduce the activating effect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the protected intermediate
Acetylation of aniline forms acetanilide (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NHCOCH_3}\)).

Step 2: Examine the resonance in acetanilide
The unshared electron pair on nitrogen is conjugated not only with the aromatic ring but also with the carbonyl group (\(\mathrm{C=O}\)): \(\mathrm{-N(lone\ pair)-C=O \longleftrightarrow -N^+=C-O^-}\).

Step 3: Evaluate the electron availability
Because the carbonyl oxygen is electronegative, resonance with the carbonyl group draws electron density away from nitrogen, making the lone pair significantly less available for donation into the benzene ring.

Conclusion:
Acetylation reduces ring activation because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen.

answer.text: Acetylation changes the hybridization of the aromatic ring carbons from \(sp^2\) to \(sp^3\)
The lone pair of electrons on nitrogen is delocalized onto the carbonyl oxygen through resonance, making it less available for donation to the benzene ring
The acetyl group acts as an ortho/para-directing activator stronger than the amino group
Acetylation prevents electrophilic attacks by destroying the aromaticity of the ring

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q39 - Significant meta product in direct nitration of aniline

questiontext.text: Direct nitration of aniline with a mixture of concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) and concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) at 288 K yields 51% \(p\)-nitroaniline, 47% \(m\)-nitroaniline, and 2% \(o\)-nitroaniline. Why is a substantial amount of the \(m\)-nitro derivative formed despite the amino group being \(o,p\)-directing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the medium conditions
Direct nitration uses concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, which is an extremely strong acidic medium.

Step 2: Analyze protonation of aniline
Under these strongly acidic conditions, a significant fraction of aniline is protonated to form the anilinium ion: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_3^+}\).

Step 3: Evaluate directing nature of the anilinium ion
In the anilinium ion, the positively charged nitrogen has a strong \(-I\) electron-withdrawing effect, deactivating the ring and directing incoming electrophiles (\(\mathrm{NO_2^+}\)) to the meta position.

Step 4: Relate to observed percentages
Electrophilic attack on the anilinium ion yields 47% meta-nitroaniline alongside the ortho/para products formed from unprotonated aniline.

Conclusion:
Substantial meta-nitroaniline is formed because aniline is protonated in strongly acidic medium to form the meta-directing anilinium ion.

answer.text: The nitronium ion undergoes nucleophilic addition preferentially at the meta carbon
Nitrous acid produced in the mixture selectively oxidizes the meta positions
In strongly acidic medium, aniline is protonated to form the anilinium ion, which is meta-directing
Steric hindrance by the amino group blocks both ortho and para positions completely

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q40 - Sulphanilic acid formation and zwitterionic structure

questiontext.text: Sulphonation of aniline with concentrated sulphuric acid followed by heating at 453-473 K yields sulphanilic acid as the major product. Sulphanilic acid exists predominantly as which dipolar species?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Trace the sulphonation reaction
Aniline reacts with concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to form anilinium hydrogensulphate, which upon heating at 453-473 K undergoes rearrangement to yield \(p\)-aminobenzenesulphonic acid (sulphanilic acid).

Step 2: Examine the functional groups in sulphanilic acid
Sulphanilic acid contains both a basic amino group (\(-\mathrm{NH_2}\)) and an acidic sulphonic acid group (\(-\mathrm{SO_3H}\)) within the same molecule.

Step 3: Describe internal proton transfer
An internal acid-base proton transfer takes place: the acidic proton of \(-\mathrm{SO_3H}\) is transferred to the basic \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group, generating the dipolar zwitterion \(\mathrm{H_3N^+-C_6H_4-SO_3^-}\).

Conclusion:
Sulphanilic acid exists as the zwitterion \(\mathrm{H_3N^+-C_6H_4-SO_3^-}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q41 - Aniline inertness in Friedel Crafts reactions

questiontext.text: Aniline does not undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation or acylation reactions when treated with an alkyl/acyl halide and anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\). What is the underlying reason?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the catalyst and reactant roles
In Friedel-Crafts reactions, anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) is employed as a Lewis acid catalyst. Aniline has an unshared electron pair on its nitrogen atom, making it a strong Lewis base.

Step 2: Examine complex formation
The lone pair on nitrogen coordinates directly with \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) to form a Lewis acid-base complex (salt): \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2 \rightarrow AlCl_3}\).

Step 3: Evaluate the effect on the aromatic ring
Due to coordination, the nitrogen atom acquires a positive formal charge. This positively charged nitrogen acts as an extremely powerful electron-withdrawing group, drastically deactivating the benzene ring toward any further electrophilic attack.

Conclusion:
Aniline fails to undergo Friedel-Crafts reactions because it forms a salt with \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), deactivating the benzene ring.

answer.text: Aniline acts as a Lewis base and forms an adduct/salt with the Lewis acid catalyst \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), acquiring a positive charge that strongly deactivates the aromatic ring
\(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) hydrolyses aniline into phenol and nitrogen gas
Aniline is completely non-nucleophilic and cannot interact with Lewis acids
Friedel-Crafts catalysts only react with aliphatic hydrocarbons

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q42 - Optimal temperature for diazotisation of aniline

questiontext.text: At what temperature range must the diazotisation of aniline with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\) be carried out to obtain benzenediazonium chloride stably in solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall reaction specifications for diazotisation
Benzenediazonium chloride is stable only for a short time in cold aqueous solution. At temperatures above \(278\,\mathrm{K}\) (above \(5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)), it readily undergoes hydrolysis with water to form phenol.

Step 2: State the required temperature
The NCERT textbook explicitly specifies that diazotisation is carried out at \(273 - 278\,\mathrm{K}\) (\(0 - 5^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)).

Conclusion:
Diazotisation is performed at \(273 - 278\,\mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q43 - Comparison of Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements correctly compares the Sandmeyer reaction with the Gattermann reaction for synthesizing chlorobenzene or bromobenzene from benzenediazonium salts?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Compare reagents
The Sandmeyer reaction introduces chlorine or bromine into the ring using cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide dissolved in the corresponding halogen acid (\(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2/HCl}\) or \(\mathrm{Cu_2Br_2/HBr}\)). The Gattermann reaction introduces halogen using copper powder in the presence of halogen acid (\(\mathrm{Cu/HCl}\) or \(\mathrm{Cu/HBr}\)).

Step 2: Compare yields
The NCERT textbook explicitly highlights: 'The yield in Sandmeyer reaction is found to be better than Gattermann reaction.'

Conclusion:
The Sandmeyer reaction uses cuprous halides and provides a better yield than the Gattermann reaction.

answer.text: Gattermann reaction employs cuprous halides and gives higher yields than the Sandmeyer reaction
Both reactions use copper powder and produce identical chemical yields

Sandmeyer reaction employs cuprous halides (\(\mathrm{Cu_2Cl_2}\) or \(\mathrm{Cu_2Br_2}\)) in halogen acids and gives better yields than the Gattermann reaction, which uses copper powder and halogen acids
Sandmeyer reaction requires alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) whereas Gattermann reaction requires concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q44 - Preparation of iodobenzene using potassium iodide

questiontext.text: How is iodobenzene conveniently synthesized from benzenediazonium chloride in high yield without the need for a copper catalyst?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the reaction for introducing iodine
Direct iodination of benzene is reversible and requires strong oxidising agents. However, benzenediazonium chloride undergoes ready nucleophilic substitution with iodide ions.

Step 2: Review the specific reagent
Simply treating the aqueous diazonium salt solution with potassium iodide (\(\mathrm{KI}\)) results in the displacement of nitrogen: \(\mathrm{ArN_2Cl + KI \rightarrow ArI + KCl + N_2}\). No cuprous catalyst is required.

Conclusion:
Iodobenzene is prepared by treating the diazonium salt solution with potassium iodide.

answer.text: By reacting with cuprous iodide in the presence of \(\mathrm{HI}\)
By refluxing aniline directly with molecular iodine
By treating the diazonium salt solution with potassium iodide (\(\mathrm{KI}\)) and warming

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q45 - Synthesis of fluorobenzene via diazonium fluoroborate

questiontext.text: Fluorobenzene is prepared by treating benzenediazonium chloride with fluoroboric acid (\(\mathrm{HBF_4}\)) to precipitate benzenediazonium fluoroborate, followed by thermal decomposition. What are the products of this thermal decomposition?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the reaction sequence
Benzenediazonium chloride reacts with \(\mathrm{HBF_4}\) to precipitate water-insoluble benzenediazonium fluoroborate: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+ Cl^- + HBF_4 \rightarrow C_6H_5N_2^+ BF_4^- + HCl}\).

Step 2: Trace the thermal decomposition
Upon dry heating, the fluoroborate salt undergoes decomposition: \(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+ BF_4^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} C_6H_5F + BF_3 + N_2}\).

Conclusion:
Thermal decomposition yields fluorobenzene, \(\mathrm{BF_3}\), and \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q46 - Reduction of diazonium salts to benzene

questiontext.text: Benzenediazonium chloride can be reduced to benzene by treatment with hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\)) or ethanol. During these reactions, what oxidation products are formed from \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\) and ethanol, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Write the redox equation with hypophosphorous acid
\(\mathrm{ArN_2^+ Cl^- + H_3PO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow ArH + N_2 + H_3PO_3 + HCl}\). Here, hypophosphorous acid (oxidation state +1) is oxidised to phosphorous acid (oxidation state +3).

Step 2: Write the redox equation with ethanol
\(\mathrm{ArN_2^+ Cl^- + CH_3CH_2OH \rightarrow ArH + N_2 + CH_3CHO + HCl}\). Here, ethanol is oxidised to ethanal (acetaldehyde).

Conclusion:
The respective oxidation products are phosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)) and ethanal (\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q47 - Azo coupling reactions forming coloured dyes

questiontext.text: Benzenediazonium chloride undergoes electrophilic coupling with phenol in basic medium and with aniline in mildly acidic medium to produce coloured azo dyes. What are the names and colours of these dyes, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine coupling with phenol
In basic medium (\(\mathrm{pH\ 9-10}\)), phenol forms phenoxide ion, which is intensely activated and couples at its para position with benzenediazonium chloride to yield \(p\)-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye.

Step 2: Examine coupling with aniline
In mildly acidic medium (\(\mathrm{pH\ 4-5}\)), aniline couples at its para position with benzenediazonium chloride to yield \(p\)-aminoazobenzene, a yellow dye.

Conclusion:
The products are \(p\)-hydroxyazobenzene (orange dye) and \(p\)-aminoazobenzene (yellow dye).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_AMINES_MCQ_Q48 - Multistep conversion of aniline to tribromobenzene

questiontext.text: Which sequence of reactions correctly accomplishes the conversion of aniline into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Exploit the activating directing effect of the amino group
Treating aniline with bromine water causes bromination at all available ortho and para positions (carbons 2, 4, and 6), yielding 2,4,6-tribromoaniline.

Step 2: Convert the amino group into a leaving diazonium group
Subjecting 2,4,6-tribromoaniline to diazotisation with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\) at \(273 - 278\,\mathrm{K}\) converts the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group into \(-\mathrm{N_2^+ Cl^-}\), producing 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride.

Step 3: Remove the diazonium group reductively
Treating 2,4,6-tribromobenzenediazonium chloride with hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\)) in water replaces the diazonium group with hydrogen, leaving bromine atoms at the 1, 3, and 5 positions to give 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.

Conclusion:
The sequence is bromination with \(\mathrm{Br_2 / H_2O}\), diazotisation with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2 / HCl}\), and reductive deamination with \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2 / H_2O}\).

answer.text: Direct bromination of benzene with \(\mathrm{Br_2 / FeBr_3}\) \(\rightarrow\) nitration \(\rightarrow\) reduction with \(\mathrm{Sn / HCl}\)
Diazotisation with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2 / HCl}\) \(\rightarrow\) reaction with \(\mathrm{Cu_2Br_2 / HBr}\) \(\rightarrow\) bromination with \(\mathrm{Br_2 / Fe}\)
Acetylation with acetic anhydride \(\rightarrow\) bromination \(\rightarrow\) alkaline hydrolysis
Bromination with bromine water \(\rightarrow\) diazotisation with \(\mathrm{NaNO_2 / HCl}\) at 273-278 K \(\rightarrow\) reductive deamination with \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2 / H_2O}\)
